title: The 5s bar draws, and a counter pick has to earn the name

items.text: The Ranked 5s bar was empty. It asked for a colour variable that was never defined, so its gradient did not parse and the fill had nothing to draw with.
The strip down the side of each Overview card is that player's own colour, the same one they carry on the charts and in the duo grid. Cards about the group rather than a person keep the house accent.

The corner mark in the duo grid is sized by how far ahead the carrying player is, scaled against the widest gap in the group, so the marks rank as well as flag. Brett and Winny is the widest at the moment.

A counter pick now has to pass three tests: the champion is played a tenth of the time or less, so a main can never be one; the matchup wins outright at 60% or better; and the margin over that player's own winrate clears what a run that short could produce by chance. Two matchups qualify across the group, where the old rule tagged Zed on 423 games.
The coverage table under Trios and five mans is gone.

title: Ranked 5s is in, and every game now knows its lane

items.text: Ranked 5s is imported: 172 games across six players, with a ladder rank for each. Riot calls that ladder RANKED_PREMADE_5x5 and the queue 710. It has its own row on every card, its own slice in the game types ring, its own column in the champion table, and it counts toward the five-man stacks.

Lane data is complete. Every one of the 2,713 games now records the position played and the champion in the opposing lane, where before only 171 did. Kirish's matchup table goes from nothing to 43 entries and the roles ring is built from every game rather than one in seventeen.
Remakes are Riot's own call now rather than a guess from game length. The duration rule was cutting games Riot does not consider remakes at all.
Rank snapshots cover Ranked 5s as well as Solo/Duo and Flex, so its trend, its peak and its LP per win will build up the same way the others did.

1,953 cache entries under the original match-id-only key are gone. Nothing could read them: every lookup is matchId|puuid, which is what stops two friends in the same game from overwriting each other's stat line.

title: A seven day trend that covers seven days

items.text: The 7 day trend kept only the snapshots that fell inside the window, which measures whatever happened to land there rather than the window itself. With readings on the 21st, 27th and 29th it compared the 27th against the 29th and called two days a week: Shas2nd showed no movement at all despite a demotion, and a fifty LP drop earlier in the week did not register. It now anchors on the last reading at or before the cutoff, which is what the rank actually was seven days ago. Shas2nd reads -42 LP and a demotion; Kirish -53; Brett +119.
The leaderboard's trend column drops the (7d) suffix, which repeated its own heading.
The header says "Data from" and its build time, and a live refresh appends when the ranks on top of it were read. The build time only moves when fetch_data.py runs, which is what a shared link shows.

fetch_data.py --prune-cache drops the 1,953 cache entries left under the original match-id-only key. Nothing can read them: every lookup uses matchId|puuid, which is what stops two friends in the same game from overwriting each other's stat line.

A --refetch-details pass that could not re-fetch a match kept the cached copy instead of dropping the game. Riot stops serving very old matches, and losing a game from the season to gain a field on it is the wrong trade.

title: Faces follow the top champion, and the key follows the live ladder

items.text: The LP per game key and the standings under it kept the order the page was published in, so after a refresh somebody who had dropped to 0 LP still sat above somebody on 26. Both now sort on the rank they are showing. The chart's own lines keep their published order, because that is what ties a line to a colour.

The rank crests are not drawn to one scale: the tier ones sit inside a 20x20 box with a margin, unranked fills a 16x16 box edge to edge, and gold is 17x13. Unranked is scaled back to the weight of a tier crest and all of them fit rather than stretch.

The queue bars started and finished at different points because the column holding the record was sized to its text, so a queue reading 0W / 0L gave the bar beside it more room than one reading 447W / 446L. Fixed width now.
The 7 day trend is Ranked Solo/Duo only, with no queue letters.
A game added by a refresh is no longer tinted blue. It fought with the shared-game colour on the same row, and a new game is a game like any other.
A card's face and background art are the top of its weighted champion table rather than highest mastery, so the picture and the table agree. Winny is Twitch rather than Samira.

The duo grid marks the corner of a cell where the player on that row holds the higher KDA across the pair's games, so reading across a row shows which pairings they carry. The KDA comparison is Solo/Duo only now, matching the grid it sits in.

Hovering "weighted" on a card spells out the rating: the player's own winrate, plus the champion's lift shrunk by games / (games + 15) and halved for its counter-pick share, plus up to 16 points for volume.

title: Ranked 5s on the cards, and rank colours that match their crests

items.text: Ranked 5s has its own row on every friend card and its own slice in the game types ring. A queue with no ladder entry still shows its record, counted off the season's own games.

Diamond's text was blue while its crest is violet. Every rank colour is now taken from the mini crest the page draws next to it. Diamond keeps the bluer half of the violet range and Master the redder, so the two stay apart in a leaderboard.
An unranked crest, so an unranked queue gets the same treatment as a ranked one instead of an empty square.

The 7 day trend used a hollow triangle for "nothing recorded", which is still an arrow shape: a card with two quiet queues read as two upward arrows. It is a grey dash now. Direction is settled first (green up for LP gained, red down for LP lost, grey dash for nothing), and only then does the distance decide the count. Each queue's group is tagged S, F or 5, since two untagged groups side by side read as one run of arrows about one thing.
Top champions and Highest mastery now share a row height, so the two tables line up down the card.
A card's face and background art are the player's highest mastery champion.

The refresh had a budget of 40 match lookups for the whole group, which a seven person list can exhaust partway down, leaving whoever came last with nothing and making it look as though only one person had played. Everyone gets their full window now, and the status line names who got new games rather than only counting them.
The Fresh badge is gone from the cards, and the snapshot count is gone from the rank progress table.

title: Ranked 5s found, and the cards lose their footnotes

items.text: Ranked 5s is queue 710. Of the three unnamed queue ids sitting in the match cache it is the only one played on Summoner's Rift at all, with a real CS per minute on all 34 of its games where every game under 1740 and 1750 has none. All 34 fall on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday and all 34 start between 19:00 and 23:59. It is back on the fetch list, so those games will import on the next run.
The ring charts have no key underneath. Hovering a segment puts its count, its share and its name in the middle of the ring instead.
The 7 day trend is one to three arrows: one up to 50 LP, two to 100, three beyond, green up or red down, one group per queue.
Rank emblems sit outside the text in the card's top corner, so the current and peak crests line up down the edge.
The four season figures run in a line above the champion tables, which gives the weighted table room enough to read without sliding it sideways.
Every champion, most played first now splits its games by queue, so a total can be checked against a site that counts a different set of them.
The paragraphs explaining how each number was worked out are gone from the page.

title: Friend cards rebuilt, and 64 remakes stop counting as games

items.text: 64 remakes were counting as real games. fetch_data.py drops them, but only for matches fetched since it started reading Riot's early-surrender flag, and 2,396 of 2,565 records here predate that. They are now spotted by duration: nothing but a remake ends inside four minutes, and there is a clean gap between the three minute remakes and the six minute stomps. Kirish's season drops from 971 games to 946 and his Zed from 401 to 393.

LP per win and per loss was wrong. It solved for one pair of numbers across every snapshot gap at once, and a single gap that could not be squared with the rest dragged the whole answer: Brett came out at 13.4 LP a loss when he actually loses about 19. It now reads the per-game steps the LP chart is already drawn from, which are fitted to land exactly on each measured snapshot. Brett is 22.0 and 18.3, and 20 wins and 8 losses at those rates comes to the +294 LP his rank really moved.

A game added by a refresh was built with eight cells where the table has nine: the "With" column was missing entirely, so every column from Champion rightwards landed one place left of its own heading. Those rows now also carry the shared-game tint, and are written only once every friend has been fetched, since a game two of them played is only recognisable as shared once both fetches are back.

Friend cards rebuilt. The ranked queues read down the left with their winrate bars, and two ring charts on the right show what the season was made of: which queue each game was played in, with Solo/Duo split by whether one of the group was on the team, and which lane it was played from. Under them, the weighted champion table, the mastery table and the season tiles sit side by side, then LP per win and per loss for every queue over the season and the last 20 games. The card header carries a trend arrow per queue.
A switch to turn the projected lines on the LP per game chart off.

Under the stacks table, an account of where everyone's Flex and Ranked 5s games went: how many were in a listed trio or five man, how many had four of them on a team (a five man whose fifth player is outside the group, since Flex has no four player party), and how many had only one or two of them. The three add up to the total, so Rory playing 28 Flex games and appearing in rows worth 18 of them is explained rather than looking like a gap.

fetch_data.py kept only RANKED_SOLO_5x5 and RANKED_FLEX_SR from Riot's ranked entries and discarded anything else. Every queue Riot returns is now carried through under its own name, and any queue in a match history that has no name yet is printed, so a ranked queue that exists can no longer be invisible.

title: A live rank reading reaches the whole page

items.text: Refreshing updated the leaderboard and nothing else. The rank in each card's top corner, the Solo/Duo row underneath it with its winrate bar and record, the card's accent colour, and the "Rank now" column under the LP chart all kept showing whatever was true when the page was built, so one screen gave two different answers to the same question. They all follow the live reading now.
The "Rank now" column only updated when the refresh also found new games, because the live reading was only fed to the chart alongside them. It is applied on its own now.
A live rank above anything on record is treated as the new peak, instead of printing a current rank with a lower peak underneath it.

title: Friend cards read like the game list

items.text: A game on a friend card that was shared with somebody else is now tinted with that pairing's own blended colour, the same treatment the game list on the Rank progress tab already had. The same duo is the same colour on both pages, so a card shows at a glance which games were played alongside one of the group and with whom. No gap between rows here: a card lists one player, so consecutive rows are always separate games rather than the two halves of one.
The four sections on each card say what they contain and in what order: Every game, newest first; Every champion, most played first; Every matchup, most played first; Every role, most played first.

title: Duos are Solo/Duo, stacks are Flex, and the game list refreshes

items.text: Rank emblems were missing everywhere. Community Dragon removed the folder the URLs pointed at, so every tier crest on the page had been 404ing. They now come from the supported path, and being SVG they are under 2 KB each instead of 230 KB.

A second refresh in the same session added the same games to a card again. The list of games already seen was read from a constant baked into the page at build time, so every game the first refresh found looked new to the second one. That list is now kept up to date as games arrive.

"Every game, newest first" never picked up games played since the page was published. The rows are ordered across all seven players at once and each carries an LP step that only exists once the whole timeline is rebuilt, so it could not be patched a row at a time. It is now rebuilt in the browser from the same data the chart is, and the self-check that guards the chart against drift covers the table too.
Every LP figure in that table had lost its green or red. The class saying which way the LP went was being overwritten by the class marking a shared game.
The champion column did not line up on tinted rows: the cell was laid out as a flex container, so it sized to its contents rather than to the row and its background sat short of the rest.

The rank progress table said "since tracking began" but tagged rows that stayed inside one division with "(30d)" and rows that changed rank with nothing. It now measures exactly the window the chart draws, and the header names it.

Duo synergy is Ranked Solo/Duo only, both the grid and the pair table. A duo is a Solo/Duo idea: two people who chose each other out of a lobby of ten. Two names on the same Flex team usually means a trio or a five man, and counting those as a pair credited a pairing with games three or five people played.

The grid's diagonal now says how many games it rests on and is coloured against an even 50%. It was the one cell with no game count and no colour, and it is the number every other cell in that row is measured against.
Synergy shows a % and says what it is: their winrate together minus the winrate those two average apart. +5% means the pair wins five games in a hundred more often than the two of them usually do.

Trios and five mans is where Flex and Ranked 5s live, and only exact lineups count. A group is only ever credited with games that exact group played: two different five mans sharing four names do not add up to a four man that never queued.

A counter pick needed a real margin. Three wins in five beats a 50% player, and that is what a coin does five times, but it was being tagged. The matchup now has to beat their overall winrate by more than a run that length could produce on its own.

LP per win and per loss was printing numbers the snapshots did not support: one player's whole reading came from a single gap recording one loss against 44 LP. It now needs three usable gaps and fifteen games, both figures have to land inside the range a ranked game can be worth, and the fit has to reproduce the gaps it came from to within a few LP a game. Gaps where nothing moved across real games, or that move more per game than a game can be worth, are thrown out rather than averaged in. Most players show a dash, which is the honest answer this early.

fetch_data.py now records the time a rank snapshot was taken, not just the date. A reading taken at midday is not a statement about that evening's games, and the LP fit sharpens on its own as timed snapshots accumulate.
Two figures on each card: how many Solo/Duo games were played with one of the group, and how many without, each with a percentage.
Lane matchups moved above role breakdown on each card.

title: Charts get a side key and a projected line; cards get matchups and LP rates

items.text: Both rank charts now put the key beside the plot with even gaps between names, instead of a row of chips above the chart and a legend below it. The season numbers move under the chart as a table: games, net LP, winrate and record, one row per player, so they can be compared down a column.

A dashed projection on the LP per game chart. Each line is extended to the game count of whoever has played most, one game at a time at that player's own winrate and their own average LP per win and per loss, so it has the ups and downs a real climb has rather than being a straight diagonal.

Every pair is now listed twice, once under each name, so either player can be found in the first column. A dot in front of each pair carries the pairing's blended colour, the same one their shared games are tinted with on the Rank progress tab.
"Boost" is now "Booster", which is what the column actually names.

The stacks table says when a party size has no games rather than leaving a gap that looks like a bug, and explains that the 5s column is the Ranked 5s queue Riot removed from the game in 2016. It is still requested on every fetch and will fill in on its own if that queue ever returns.
Each friend card shows their current Solo/Duo rank in the top right with the emblem and LP, and their season peak beneath it.

A Top Champions section above Highest Mastery. The rating starts from that player's own winrate, adds how far each champion beats it (pulled back toward nothing while the sample is small, and halved for the share of games played in matchups that champion is already favoured in), then adds up to 16 points for volume. Games and winrate on their own each pick the wrong champion.

LP per win and per loss, for Solo/Duo and Flex, across the tracked window and across the last 50 games. Riot never reports the LP change for one game, so this is solved from the rank snapshots: every gap between two of them gives one equation, and the two figures are fitted across all of them. A queue without at least two differently shaped gaps shows a dash rather than a guess.

A lane matchups table per player: winrate and average KDA on each champion against each opposing laner faced five or more times, tagged a counter pick where they win it more often than they win in general. Riot only returns the lane opponent with the full match detail, so games cached before that was collected do not carry it; the table says how much of the season it covers, and fetch_data.py --refetch-details fills in the rest.
The nemesis line is gone. One champion's name and a loss count said less than the matchup table now answers with a winrate and a KDA beside it.

title: Shared games read as one game

items.text: The stripe on a shared game was built starting from each row's own player, so the two rows of one game drew the same colours in opposite order and the bar flipped halfway down. Each pairing now has one blended colour that looks the same wherever it appears.

A shared game is drawn as a single block: the line between its rows is removed and a gap follows it, so a long duo queue session reads as a run of separate games rather than one continuous tinted stretch.

The stacks table no longer invents groups of four. Flex takes one, two, three or five, so four of you on a team is somebody else's five man with four of you in it. Only trios and five mans are listed, and the queue columns are Flex and 5s rather than a Solo column that can never have anything in it.

title: One key per chart, and who carries whom

items.text: Champions whose name has an apostrophe or a space had no icon anywhere, because the icon list is keyed by display name while match data reports Riot's internal key. K'Sante, Kai'Sa, Cho'Gath, Wukong and the rest now resolve, which is why Neel had no face. All 111 champions in your season now have one.

Both charts drop the stack of names beside the lines. The legend underneath was already the key, so that was the same key drawn twice, and it now carries the LP moved and the rank change. The chart gets the freed width.
Promotions in the game by game table say how much LP the game was worth, and read Promoted rather than promoted.
The stripe on a shared game is made from the colours of the players who were in it, so it says who you were with rather than only that you were with someone.
The 7 day trend column shows the LP travelled alongside a rank change.

Boost now compares the two players inside the games they played together, rather than each of them against their own average elsewhere. Same games, same map, same opponents, same result, so the comparison is like for like.
The stacks table no longer calls four players a four stack. Flex cannot be queued as four, so four of you on a team is a five man whose fifth player is not in this group; those rows are marked +1.
Standings chips above the chart are back to rank and games, with the movement in the legend where it is not repeated three times.

title: Dark only, sortable duo tables, and stacks

items.text: Light mode is gone. One theme means one value per colour instead of two.
A Trios and full stacks table: lineups of three or more on the same team, counted as whole lineups rather than every pair inside them. Your best is Kirish, Winny, Shas and Brett at 75% over 12 games.
A Boost column on the pair table: whose own KDA improves most when playing alongside the other. Shas2nd averages 3.99 KDA with Winny against 2.44 otherwise.
Both duo tables sort by any column now. Pairs open alphabetically rather than in an order that asserts something, and stacks open by games played.
Two more numbers in This week at a glance: who is on the hottest streak, and how many of the week's games had two or more of them on the same team.
The chart keys drop the dashed leader lines, and each name carries both the LP moved and the rank change instead of only one of the two.
Games played together are banded down the left of the game by game table, so a shared game reads as one game rather than two rows with the same timestamp.
Days a rank moved says how much LP the move was worth, not just that a promotion happened.

Player faces and card art come from the champion most played this season rather than lifetime mastery, which kept showing champions nobody had touched all split. The mastery list is now labelled Highest mastery champions.

title: A cleaner chart, and faces for everyone

items.text: The LP chart no longer scatters dots along the lines. Only the end of each line is marked; every game is still there as an invisible point, so hovering anywhere on a line brings up that game.

The names beside the chart are one line each instead of two, and the movement that used to sit under them has gone to the standings chips above. That also takes the last green and red text out of the chart, so a name's colour only ever means who it is.

Player colours no longer include green or red. Those mean won and lost everywhere else, so a player whose colour was green sat in a table row next to a green "+22 LP" and the colour stopped saying which of the two it meant.
Everyone has a face now: their most mastered champion, on their card, on their button, and in the leaderboard.
The Friends buttons filter again, with an All friends button to bring everyone back. Pressing the person you are already on also returns to All.
Long dashes are gone from the writing across the site.

title: A readable LP chart, and duo games marked

items.text: Biggest climber now shows the LP behind a promotion. "Platinum I → Emerald IV" tells you how far someone went but not how much, it now reads "Platinum I → Emerald IV +97 LP", counted across the tier change rather than from the league points that reset at a promotion.
Games this week moved out of the season totals and into This week at a glance, with the rest of the week.

The LP chart no longer puts a green or red dot on every game. Four hundred of them buried the seven lines and fought the per-player colours for nothing, a step upward already tells you the game was won. Only the measured daily snapshots are drawn as markers now; the games between them are faint points in the player's own colour, and hovering any of them still gives the full game.
Tier lines on the chart are drawn firmly and the divisions between them faintly, instead of ten identical lines behind the data.
Games played alongside another tracked player are marked with a "With" column in both the game-by-game table and each player's match list, naming whoever was on their team in that game.
The rank emblem in the rank progress table was invisible because its cell had been dropped out of the table's column layout.

title: Friends, Overview and the rank tables

items.text: The Friends tab shows everyone at once. The buttons across the top now jump to a player and ring their card instead of hiding the other six, so you can still compare people. Press the same button again to clear it.
Rank emblems now sit on each player, on their card, on their button, and beside every rank in the tables.
Platinum and Emerald were two shades of the same green, which made the two most common ranks in this group hard to tell apart anywhere on the site. Platinum is now the turquoise it has in game.

Overview leads with the leaderboard, then this week, then highlights, and carries a row of group totals: games and hours this season and this week, the combined winrate, and how many different champions have been played.
The game-by-game table under the LP chart is one list for everyone, newest game first, instead of being grouped by player with today's games buried at the bottom of a block.

The rank progress table listed every daily snapshot for every player, so hundreds of rows read "–" in the Change column. It now shows only the days a rank actually moved, twenty rows instead of several hundred.

title: The duo table ranks by synergy

items.text: The full pair table is ordered by synergy rather than by games played, and now has a synergy column to order by, it was sorted by volume with no synergy figure shown at all. Each pair gets a bar growing out from the centre: right of the line means the two do better together than apart, left means worse.
Player names carry their chart colours, the pairs are numbered, and the solo and flex splits sit alongside the totals.
Pairs with fewer than ten games are marked and sorted to the bottom, so a lucky five-game run can no longer sit at the top as the best pairing.

title: Newly generated API keys are no longer rejected

items.text: Riot refuses a development key for up to a minute after issuing it. The key box treated that as "expired, generate a fresh one", advice that produces another key which behaves the same way, so every key you made looked rejected. It now retries before believing the rejection, and says to wait rather than to generate another.
A key entered in one tab is now picked up by other tabs left open, instead of those tabs carrying on with the old one and still reporting it as rejected.

title: Duo synergy rebuilt as a grid

items.text: Duo synergy was missing most of its games. It only counted a pair when both players' records carried a team id, and only about one match in ten does, so Brett and Winny showed 6 games together instead of 130, and ten pairs including Neel and Winny did not appear at all. It now works out who was on the same team from the result, which every record has.

The table is now a grid of everyone against everyone. The number is a pair's winrate together; the colour is whether that beats how often those two win apart, so green means the pairing actually helps. The diagonal is each player on their own, which is the number every cell in that row is being compared against.
Tap any square for that pair's full record. Under the grid, a line calls out the best and worst pairings and the most played.

Split by queue: all queues, Solo/Duo only, or Flex only. Everything follows the choice, including the comparison against each player's usual winrate, which is worked out separately per queue. Several pairs only exist in one, Neel and Winny's 20 games together are all Flex.
Pairs with fewer than ten games together are shown but left uncoloured, because a winrate over five games says more about luck than about the pair.
Remade games (the early-surrender kind that count for nothing) were being included in duo records. They are excluded everywhere else and now here too.

The duo grid now says how far back each player's match history reaches. A pairing can only be spotted in a game that is inside both players' histories, and those start on different dates, so two people can have played together without it showing up here.

title: Refreshing now updates games and the LP chart

items.text: Refresh ranks only ever updated the leaderboard's rank and record. Everyone's Form dots and recent match list stayed on whatever was published, so a refresh looked like it had done nothing. It now pulls each player's new ranked games too, and marks them so you can see what arrived.
The LP per game chart now redraws with those new games as well, and the standings above it follow. Your zoom setting and any lines you have hidden survive the redraw.

The leaderboard is ordered when the page is built, so a refresh used to update everyone's LP without moving them, leaving #1 on 80 LP sitting above #2 on 26 LP. Rows now re-sort and renumber, medals included, and each player's card badge follows.
Season totals and the champion breakdown still come from the published snapshot, those need a player's whole season, which a browser cannot rebuild. The status line says what did and did not move.

title: Patch notes

items.text: This panel. The sparkle button in the header lists what has changed on the dashboard, and shows a dot when there is something you have not read yet.

title: Links to op.gg, u.gg and League of Graphs

items.text: Every friend card now has op.gg, u.gg and League of Graphs links under the player's Riot ID, each opening in a new tab.

title: Refreshing and the API key are separate buttons

items.text: Refresh ranks now uses your saved key and goes, instead of stopping to ask for a key every single time.
The API key button handles the key on its own, and checks it against Riot before saving, so a bad or expired key is caught right there rather than half way through a refresh.
A Forget saved key option, for when someone else uses your computer.
When Riot rejects a key it is now cleared automatically, so the next refresh asks for a new one instead of failing the same way with no explanation.
Choosing not to remember a key now keeps it for the rest of your visit, rather than forgetting it immediately and asking again seconds later.

title: Riot API key box rebuilt

items.text: Ticking "Remember this key" and then mistyping the key wiped the tickbox, so the key was silently never saved.

Pasting a new key over an old one joined the two together. That still started with RGAPI-, so it was accepted and Riot answered with a confusing 401. The whole key is now checked, and the box selects itself so a paste replaces what is there.
developer.riotgames.com is a real link you can click, instead of a line of text you had to retype.
Redesigned box: the key is shown in a monospaced font so a wrong character stands out, errors say what is actually wrong, and the buttons are finger sized on a phone.

title: A proper look

items.text: An icon in the browser tab, and a preview card when the link is shared into Discord or WhatsApp showing the current top five.
Each player's most played champion now sits as artwork behind the top of their card, tinted with their rank colour.
Three of the header buttons had no styling at all and rendered as plain grey browser buttons next to the styled ones.
Tidier header, scrollbars that match the theme, and a real footer.

title: Getting around the dashboard

items.text: The address bar now follows what you are looking at, so you can send someone a link that opens straight on a player or on the rank chart.
The back button moves between tabs instead of leaving the site.
The tab bar stays on screen as you scroll, whole leaderboard rows are clickable rather than just the name, and there is a back to top button.
On a phone the player buttons scroll along one row instead of stacking three rows deep and pushing everything down the screen.
Arrow keys move between tabs and between players.
